questions.q: Which two real technologies does this lesson describe for backing an FCI's shared storage?
options: A SAN reached via iSCSI or Fibre Channel, and Storage Spaces Direct (S2D)
Local disks in each node with no shared visibility at all
Cloud-only storage with no on-prem option
USB-attached external drives shared via a network share
questions.explain: A SAN over iSCSI/Fibre Channel is the traditional option; S2D is the modern hyper-converged alternative that pools local disks.

questions.q: What is Storage Spaces Direct (S2D), per this lesson?
options: A hyper-converged approach that pools local disks across cluster nodes into shared, resilient storage
A cloud-only backup destination
A type of Fibre Channel switch
A SQL Server backup compression algorithm
questions.explain: S2D removes the need for a separate SAN by pooling the nodes' own local disks into shared storage.

questions.q: At any given moment, how many FCI cluster nodes are actually mounting and writing to the shared volume?
options: Exactly one — the active node
All nodes simultaneously, for redundancy
None — the storage stays unmounted between failovers
Exactly two, active and one designated backup
questions.explain: Only the active node has the shared volume mounted and is writing to it; passive nodes are deliberately kept from touching it.

questions.q: What is a 'split-brain' scenario, in the context of FCI shared storage?
options: Two nodes both believing they own and can write to the same shared storage at the same time
A single node running two SQL Server instances at once
A backup job that fails halfway through
A network cable being physically disconnected with no cluster impact
questions.explain: Split-brain is when isolated nodes disagree about who owns the storage, risking simultaneous, conflicting writes and corruption.

questions.q: Why is it architecturally unsafe for both an active and a passive node to write to the same shared volume at once, even briefly?
options: Simultaneous, uncoordinated writes to the same data and log files from two nodes risks corrupting the database
It's actually completely safe and is how AGs work
SQL Server automatically merges conflicting writes with no risk
Shared storage physically prevents more than one connection at the hardware level
questions.explain: Because there's only one copy of the data, two nodes writing to it independently and uncoordinated is exactly the corruption risk shared-storage design and quorum exist to prevent.
